name: Berawan, Long Terawan dialect
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Clayre, Beatrice with Denny Belawing Wan. 1996. An introduction to Berawan phonology. The Sarawak Museum Journal L(71): 209-240. DOI 10.61507/smj22-1996-XLTF-14.
catalog_locator: p. 212, section 2.0 'The Berawan Word' (page 5 of the publisher's 5-page open preview)
catalog_quote: The minimum word in Berawan consists of one nuclear syllable (S). ... The maximum expansion of a word consists of a nuclear syllable preceded by one or two pre-nuclear syllables (s). The typical word consists of two syllables. No word longer than three syllables was recorded. Three-syllable words usually consist of a two-syllable root plus a prefix. ... The nuclear syllable (S) is the ultimate syllable of the word. It is the only syllable in which all the vowel phonemes (except schwa) may occur and it is also the location of length contrasts in both vowels and consonants. Since long consonants and long vowels occur only in S they are not analysed as full phonemes of the language, but rather as a feature, or prosody, of the nuclear syllable. Stress in Berawan falls on the nuclear syllable (S). It is marked by length and by higher, often rising, pitch, and not by high average amplitude. The same pattern was also recognized in sentence utterances (see García-Bellido and Clayre 1997 §4.1.3. and Fig. 5b).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (5 pages, text; extracted text). PDF page 5 carries the running head "212 THE SARAWAK MUSEUM JOURNAL" and section "2.0. THE BERAWAN word". The quoted passage is there word for word: "The nuclear syllable (S) is the ultimate syllable of the word. It is the only syllable in which all the vowel phonemes (except schwa) may occur and it is also the location of length contrasts in both vowels and consonants." then (elided by the compiler "[..]") "Since long consonants and long vowels occur only in S they are not analysed as full phonemes of the language, but rather as a feature, or prosody, of the nuclear syllable." then "Stress in Berawan falls on the nuclear syllable (S). It is marked by…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final (ultimate) syllable, which Clayre calls the nuclear syllable; it is the only syllable that carries the full vowel inventory and the vowel/consonant length contrasts. Stress is cued by length and by higher, often rising pitch rather than amplitude. Burkhardt 2006 (pp. 8, 15), from his own Long Terawan field data, confirms: stress 'always falls on the nucleus of the ultima', whether that nucleus is a short or long vowel, and is entirely predictable; the penultimate nucleus is always short.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in either Clayre & Wan 1996 (pp. 209-212 seen) or Burkhardt 2006. Words are maximally three syllables (usually disyllabic root + prefix).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Clayre & Wan note the analysis rests on one speaker and limited data and is preliminary, particularly regarding diphthongs; Burkhardt 2006 argues Clayre's nuclear-rhyme notion under-predicts stress in some vowel sequences and reanalyses them (e.g. /sapa:w/ 'roof', /mu.i/ 'wash') so that stress is uniformly on the ultima.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, from ~800 elicited words (citation forms) of one Long Terawan speaker analysed with CECIL; the authors state the same pattern was recognized in recorded sentences/frames but no detailed phrase-level study was made.
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted sources describe the Long Terawan dialect (Tutoh River), which Kroeger's Sarawak classification and Glottolog equate with West Berawan west2564 (ISO zbw). Note Glottolog files Clayre & Wan 1996 under east2486 (East Berawan) and Burkhardt 2006/2008 under cent2098 (Central Berawan); both papers state explicitly that they describe Long Terawan, so they belong to west2564. Clayre & Wan's analysis rests on one speaker (Denny Belawing Wan, aged 34, Long Terawan).

sources.note: Sect. 5.1 'Word Stress and Clayre's notion of the nuclear rhyme', p. 8: 'Clayre (1996:212) states that stress in LTB falls on the ultimate syllable, an observation that I share.' Conclusion p. 15: 'The above generalization makes stress placement in LTB entirely predictable: it always falls on the nucleus of the ultima, which is either a short vowel (V) or a long one (V:).' Penultimate nucleus is always short (p. 9). Author's own field data from Long Terawan speakers.

tone.says: From the citing works: a prosodic-weight analysis of the Berawan (LTN) word - onsets carry weight, geminate consonants belong to the onset of the stressed ultimate syllable, gaps in segment combinations explained by prosodic constraints (Burkhardt 2014:17-18; Burkhardt 2006:2). Clayre & Wan 1996:212 cite its sec. 4.1.3 and Fig. 5b for the finding that final-syllable stress 'is marked by length and by higher, often rising, pitch, and not by high average amplitude', in words and in sentence utter…
